## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating this aircraft through its keystone misleads in five places, and the first is the sharpest.**

### The Exchange Ratio Is Not a Property of the Aircraft

**The apparatus of this article treats the exchange ratio as a measurement, but it is better understood as a joint measurement of an aircraft, a pilot, a tactic, an adversary and a set of rules.**
The programme's own data proves it. The same aircraft in the same simulator, from a nominally identical
defensive start, returned 1.2 in one campaign and 0.47 in the next, and the programme
[attributed the difference][ref_joyce_pdf] to which initial move the pilots chose.

**A number that moves by a factor of two and a half when the pilots change their minds does not describe the airframe.**

### The Adversary Chooses the Engagement

**The F-15C and F-16C result is the boundary of the entire keystone.** An advantage that exists inside a
slow, close fight is realisable only if the opponent enters one. Against aircraft with enough excess thrust
to sit above the fight and re-enter at their chosen moment, the X-31's advantage was largely unavailable.

**The lesson is old, as the [NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] observes**, drawing the parallel with the [Fokker Dr I][ref_dr1]
of 1917, an aircraft capable of post-stall pointing that pilots of faster conventional fighters learned to
defeat by extending and attacking in slashing passes, denying it the ability to choose the time and place of
the fight.

### The Demonstrator Was Underpowered

**The X-31 fought the F/A-18 from a position of disadvantage in conventional performance**, and the
[NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] is direct about it, attributing an exchange ratio of 0.37 without post-stall technology to the basic
mediocrity of an underpowered design against a more powerful opponent with a better dogfighting wing.

**The handicap cuts both ways, and the second direction is the more interesting.** An aircraft that loses almost
three fights in four conventionally and wins nearly two in one with post-stall technology has demonstrated a
large effect. But it has demonstrated it on an airframe whose conventional performance nobody would accept,
and the programme's [own conclusion][ref_joyce_pdf] is that post-stall technology must be an integrated element of a design
rather than a bolt-on.

### The Angle of Attack Limit Is Not the Whole Capability

The article has treated the usable angle of attack as the figure of merit, because it sets the
aim-off angle. **The programme's [conclusions][ref_joyce_pdf] put velocity-vector roll rate alongside it**, and describe
the main advantages as apparent directional nose-pointing rate, which is actually yaw rate or
velocity-vector roll capability at high angle of attack, together with very high nose authority in pitch.

**Pointing where you cannot get to quickly is worth less than the static aim-off angle suggests**, and a
full treatment would need the rate as well as the angle. The rate is not published in a form this article
could use.

### The Simulation and Flight Numbers Are Not the Same Experiment

**The exchange ratios analysed at length in this article are simulation results**, from Pinball I and
Pinball II. The flight programme reported 407 engagements of which 325 were scored, and its summary
conclusions are stated qualitatively. **The temptation to read the simulator's 1.83 as a flight result should be resisted**,
and the widely quoted figures of thirty to one and of nearly ten to one over 103 dogfights come from yet
other accountings. The [NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] reports that the first close-in-combat flight campaign
comprised 103 engagements, 94 of them scorable, and that the X-31 won 64 of the 66 decided engagements from
neutral starts, a ratio of 32 to one, which is the likely origin of both figures, although neither figure
as quoted states that accounting.

**That inconsistency is itself the finding.** A programme whose keystone was a measured rate produced at
least four different headline rates that circulate independently, and the arithmetic above shows why that is
easy. The pooled value depends on the mix of starting conditions, and nobody quoting a single number says
which mix produced it.

**The condition under which pooling reverses a conclusion can be written down.** A set of per-condition
ratios supports a claim of advantage on average while the pooled figure denies it whenever

$$
\frac{1}{N} \sum_i E_i > 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_i w_i E_i < 1
\tag{71}
$$

which is possible for any set that contains at least one ratio below parity, because the weights are free.
For the published set the two sides are 6.43 and 1.83, so the first inequality is satisfied with room to spare
and the second fails by a margin of only 0.83.
**The margin is what the knife-edge calculation above measures**, and it is smaller than the uncertainty in
the weights. The general form of that hazard is known in statistics as
[the reversal that can occur when groups are pooled][ref_simpson].

## The Source Base

**The research survey holds 6,684 research records drawn from the NASA Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center through its registered identifiers, and the Crossref registry across journal and conference literature**, of which 669 are report primaries, being 10.0 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2017.** Of the 6,671 dated records, 2,428 were published through 1999 and 3,922 from 2015 onward. **Every record the survey holds is cited**, in a cluster row of The Contemporary Literature.

| Period | Records | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Before 1985 | 745 | 11.2 percent |
| **1985 to 1996, the programme window** | **1,469** | **22.0 percent** |
| 1997 to 2014 | 544 | 8.1 percent |
| 2015 onward | 3,922 | 58.7 percent |
| of which 2022 onward | 1,789 | 26.8 percent |

### Where the Programme's Own Literature Lives

**The X-31 was reported almost entirely at meetings rather than in journals**, at the meetings of the
American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics and the Society of Experimental Test Pilots and at the 1994
High Alpha Conference. The tactical utility paper the keystone rests on and the close-in-combat results
assessment published a decade after the programme ended are both conference papers.
**The vehicle's own literature cluster holds 36 records, 28 of them from the 1985 to 1996 programme window and none published from 2015 onward**, and two of them appeared in a journal.

### The Equations That Carry No Citation, and Why

**Seven displayed relations in this article carry no nearby citation and that is deliberate.** They are the
weighting identity, the two ends of the two-point bracket derived from it, displayed separately, the tipping weight, the same bracket applied
to the other two comparisons, the flight-rate bookkeeping, and the ratio between the two simulation
campaigns.

**Every one of those is a construction original to this article rather than a result taken from a source.**
Attaching a citation to them would be false attribution, and leaving them bare is the correct treatment. The
underlying arithmetic is elementary and the reader can check it, which is the point of displaying it.

**The distinction matters because the rest of the article's equations are not like that.** The atmosphere,
the thrust lapse, the lift-curve slope, the drag polar, the turn relations, the binomial interval and the
divergence eigenvalue are all standard results with a literature behind them, and each carries it.

### On the Primary Record

**The primary record for this aircraft is unusually good in one respect and unusually poor in another.** The
flight reports, the quasi-tailless results, the yawing-moment asymmetry analysis and the tactical utility
paper are all public, detailed and quantitative. The NASA history published in 2014 carries a complete
per-flight log for both aircraft and the simulation exchange ratios by starting condition.

**What is not public is the count of decided outcomes behind each simulation ratio**, which is the one
thing needed to attach an interval to any of the published ratios without assumption. The NASA history gives
48 simulated engagements for each case and counts of decided outcomes by starting condition for the flight
campaigns, but it reports the simulation results as exchange ratios and percentage increases. This article works
around that by asking what various sample sizes would support rather than by guessing which one applied.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **17 of the 36 records in the vehicle's own literature are report primaries under that rule.** The rule does not reach the conference papers in which the X-31 was mostly reported, so 10.0 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

**The programme window is the row that matters for primacy**, because it holds the work published while this
aircraft was being designed, built and flown. A record from 1993 about high angle of attack aerodynamics is
a primary source for this article in a way that a review from 2021 is not, however good the review.

### Thin Subjects

**Ten subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group, and where it offers an alternative with the word or, either suffices.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the exchange ratio as a reported quantity | exchange ratio, kill ratio, loss exchange | 6 |
| agility metrics | agility metric, agility metrics | 17 |
| the velocity-vector roll | velocity-vector roll | 6 |
| turn performance and corner speed | corner speed, corner velocity, turn rate, turn radius, turning rate, turning radius, turn performance | 6 |
| the Herbst manoeuvre | Herbst, J-turn | 7 |
| control power | control power | 12 |
| thrust lapse with altitude | thrust lapse, or engine thrust, turbofan, turbojet, jet engine together with altitude | 4 |
| carefree handling | carefree | 10 |
| the icing or blockage of an air data probe | pitot, Kiel, air data, probe together with ice, icing, blockage, blocked | 21 |
| international collaboration in aircraft development | international collaboration, international cooperation, multinational, cooperative aircraft, cooperative development | 1 |

**The quantity the keystone rests on is almost never the subject of a title.** The exchange ratio, the kill ratio and the loss exchange together appear in six titles, so the aggregation and the intervals derived in this article rest on the statistics of proportions rather than on a literature of the measure itself.

**Agility metrics are a literature of the programme's own decade.** Of the 17 titles that name them, 14 date from 1985 to 1996 and one from 2015 onward, so the vocabulary the pointing argument needs was settled then, and the one modern title is a review of it.

**The velocity-vector roll is named in six titles, all from 1985 to 1996**, the decade in which the X-31 made it the command variable of lateral stick, so the kinematics above rest on the standard axis relations rather than on a modern literature.

**Turn performance is a standard relation rather than a measured literature here.** Turn rate, turn radius, turning performance and corner speed together appear in six titles, so the turn-radius comparison above rests on the relations it displays.

**The manoeuvre that carries Herbst's name has seven titles**, and the four published from 2015 onward are all control designs for flying it.

**Control power is thin as a title term and not as a subject.** Twelve titles name control power, six of them from the programme window, while the cluster on control power and effector sizing holds 60 records, because most of its titles name control authority, control margins or control derivatives instead. **The gap is in the vocabulary rather than in the work.**

**The thrust-lapse model that the departure and altitude arguments rest on is used rather than studied.** Thrust lapse, or engine thrust together with altitude, appears in four titles, none of which names thrust lapse, which is why the lapse exponent is carried explicitly above and the sensitivity to it reported.

**Carefree handling has ten titles**, three of them on helicopters, and one, a flight demonstration of tactile cueing, takes up the problem the X-31 pilots named, of restoring the cues that carefree handling removes.

**Pitot icing was described in 1938 and became a literature only after the accident.** Of the 21 titles that join a pitot, Kiel or air data probe to ice or blockage, the earliest is from 1938, the next from 2013, and 19 were published from 2015 onward.

**One title names international collaboration or a multinational or cooperative aircraft programme**, so the statement that the arrangement was itself a first rests on the programme's own record.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Control also names the control of power grids, gene therapy and bankruptcy law, structure also names crystal structure, vehicle stability also names the stability of cars, and manoeuvrability also names the manoeuvring of ships. Tailless also names cats, rats, batrachians and whipscorpions, and canard also names the foie gras duck. A delta wing is also a vortex generator in a heat exchanger and the cause of wind loads on a canopy roof, time of flight is also a measurement of particle detectors, cameras and cytometry, departure also names an airport lounge and a gate queue, binomial also names a waveguide transformer and an optical window, agility also names the agility of an organisation, upset also names a soft error in a memory cell, and carefree also names a way of life. Diesel combustion and exhaust, power transmission cables, radio-frequency calibration, buildings and bridges, and the timing of missile launches as a question of international relations are excluded on the same rule. Correction, withdrawal and retraction notices and addenda are excluded as well, because a notice of that kind is a part of the work it concerns rather than a research work of its own, and so are book reviews, conference reports, whole proceedings volumes, special-section introductions, numbered abstract-digest entries, figure and table records, software packages, teaching datasets, encyclopedia entries, news notes and meeting minutes. A second deposit of a document already counted, such as a report-series copy of a journal paper, is not admitted either, so that each work is counted once.

**The two residual clusters are held to a stricter rule.** The general control literature keeps the flight control of aircraft and flight vehicles, and general control theory only where it is the theory this article's argument uses, being the control of statically unstable plants, robustness, gain scheduling, saturation, nonlinear and high angle of attack control, thrust-vector control, handling qualities and pilot-vehicle interaction. It excludes control in other application domains, among them robots, ground and marine vehicles, power systems including the electrical power of aircraft, communications, process plants and traffic management, and pure theory tied to none of those uses. The other aerodynamic and flight mechanics literature keeps only the aerodynamics and flight mechanics of aircraft and flight vehicles, and excludes orbital manoeuvring, engine internals, aircraft subsystems, air traffic and target tracking. **The same exclusions are applied to every other cluster** for the kinds they name, being spacecraft and orbital manoeuvring, engine internals, the electrical power and electronics of aircraft, air traffic and airline operations, robots, marine and ground vehicles, multi-agent coordination, process and networked control, fluid mechanics and acoustics without a flight vehicle, and aircraft subsystems and ergonomics. Thrust-vector control of spacecraft is kept beside thrust vectoring, and ice protection beside air data and icing. **Every cluster is also held to the argument.** A record is kept when it bears on a subject this article's argument uses, and a method or phenomenon the argument relies on is kept when it is studied on another vehicle. A record whose only link is general aeronautics is excluded, among them structural health monitoring and the integrity, manufacture and repair of airframes, the design and sizing of transports, general aviation, electric and small unmanned aircraft, propellers, distributed and electric propulsion and engine internals, aircraft noise and the sonic boom, weapon bays and store separation, command and control and mission planning, orbit change, and civil operations. Aeroelasticity, buffet and high-temperature materials, inlet distortion and nozzles, and fighter and unmanned combat aircraft design are kept. A record whose only link is a shared word of control theory or a distant domain is excluded on the same rule, among them the stability theory of switched, positive, fractional-order and delayed systems with no flight plant, controllers shown only on laboratory rigs, the dynamics and control of structures that are not aircraft, simulator motion platforms, control loaders and other ground equipment, counter-drone tasks, infrared and radar signatures, radomes and the hydraulic and engine subsystems, and the reporting of atmospheric turbulence. The control of unstable plants with time delay or actuator saturation, motion cueing as it bears on handling qualities, and missile guidance against any target are kept.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Records from other fields that share a method with the analysis in this article are kept, among them Lanchester models of ground battles and other combat effectiveness models beside the measure of effectiveness, interval estimation and sample-size work from medicine and economics beside the binomial intervals. The otter board of a trawl, studied as a low aspect ratio wing at high angle of attack, is kept beside the lift-curve section. Aviation physiology and pitot measurement outside aircraft are kept on the same reasoning, and a reader may weigh each of them accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, from the primary and official record.**

- Two aircraft were built by Rockwell International and Messerschmitt-Bolkow-Blohm and flew from
  October 1990 to June 1995, logging 580 flights with fourteen pilots, as the
  [Dryden fact sheet][ref_nasa_fs] records.
- The programme was managed by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and flown by an
  International Test Organization at NASA Dryden, and was the first experimental aircraft
  programme administered by a United States agency as an international effort.
- Controlled flight at seventy degrees of angle of attack was achieved on 6 November 1992, and a
  minimum-radius one-hundred-and-eighty-degree post-stall turn on 29 April 1993.
- The first aircraft was lost on 19 January 1995 following ice accretion on an unheated Kiel
  probe, with the pilot ejecting and being [injured on landing][ref_joyce_pdf].
- The published simulation exchange ratios against the F/A-18 with post-stall technology are 0.36,
  8.5, 16 and 0.86 across four starting conditions, with an overall figure of 1.83.
- The tactical utility flight test flew 87 sorties of which 80 were scored, producing 407
  engagements of which 325 were [scored][ref_joyce_pdf].
- The quasi-tailless demonstration reached a time to double amplitude of 290 milliseconds at
  complete simulated tail removal at a [supersonic condition][research_huberpeter_schellengerharveyg_1994].
- The second aircraft flew again from 2001 to 2003 in a separate programme with a flush air data
  system.

**Engineering analysis performed for this article.**

- The pooled exchange ratio is the mean of the per-condition ratios weighted by the losses of the
  denominator side. This is an identity, and it holds for every set of counts in which each
  condition records at least one loss on the denominator side.
- Between 81.9 and 93.6 percent of the aircraft's simulated losses must have occurred in the two
  starting conditions where it was behind. The bracket is derived analytically from two-point
  mixtures and confirmed by Monte Carlo over twenty-seven thousand feasible weight vectors, which
  ran from 0.8198 to 0.9356.
- At twelve scored outcomes per condition the defensive and high-speed line-abreast results do not
  separate from parity. The high-speed line-abreast ratio of 0.86 would need 691 scored outcomes
  to separate, against the twelve per condition and case the simulation design allowed.
- The loop gain on the accident flight stood between 2.890 and 12.543 times its design value,
  against a conventional gain margin factor of 1.995.
- The displayed airspeed and the vane angle of attack disagreed by 11.2 degrees at the moment the
  pilot remarked on them, corresponding to a dynamic-pressure error of 2.266, which already
  exceeded the design gain margin.
- Vectored control authority at thirty thousand feet is 0.6462 of its value at twenty thousand at
  the same calibrated airspeed, a loss of 35.4 percent.
- The post-stall regime offers no turn-radius advantage. Every radius computed at seventy degrees
  of angle of attack exceeds the 1,171 feet available at corner speed.
- The energy given up in a post-stall reversal from corner speed at 20,000 feet is 8,630 feet of
  specific energy and takes 46.0 seconds to recover, integrated.
- Against the steady asymmetry bound of 0.080, no arm shorter than the fuselage could hold the
  asymmetry above 237.6 knots calibrated at 20,000 feet or above 191.0 knots at 30,000 feet.

**Inference, where the record supports a conclusion without stating it.**

- The moment arm from the centre of gravity to the vane station is not determined by the flight
  record. The departure on the second aircraft, at an asymmetry of 0.125 at 35,000 feet and Mach
  0.4, bounds it below 36.2 feet under the thrust-lapse model, which the fuselage length already
  guarantees, and the bound moves from 27.1 to 48.4 feet across lapse exponents of 0.8 to 1.2. The
  17.57 feet implied by the stations a dynamic-model study tabulates lies within that bound.
- The lift-curve slope of 2.769 per radian is inferred from a test pilot's recollection of a trim
  point rather than from published data, and is supported by falling between the unswept and
  swept low-aspect-ratio estimates.
- The altitude dependence of vectored authority is offered as the quantitative explanation of an
  effect the flight-test report describes qualitatively. The report does not make the connection.

**Claims the record does not settle.**

- **The number of engagements behind each published exchange ratio is not public**, so every
  interval in this article is conditional on an assumed sample size.
- **Two widely circulated figures are not stated in the primary record in the form in which they circulate.**
  They are approximately thirty to one, and nearly ten to one over 103 dogfights. Neither is among
  the simulation figures analysed here. The NASA history reports 32 to one from neutral starts in a
  first flight campaign of 103 engagements, which is the likely origin of both, but the provenance
  of the quoted forms is unresolved.
- **The effect of an airframe with adequate conventional performance is unknown.** The
  programme's own conclusion that post-stall technology must be integrated rather than added
  implies the exchange ratio would have differed.
- The yaw inertia is not given in the flight reports, so the directional stiffness of the
  simulated tailless configuration rests on the inertia a dynamic-model study tabulates for the
  full-scale aircraft.
- The velocity-vector roll rate achieved at seventy degrees of angle of attack is described
  qualitatively in the sources consulted and no usable figure was found, so the pointing analysis
  in this article treats the angle and not the rate.
- **The basis of the 2004 close-in-combat results assessment was not established.** Whether it
  reports flight or simulation figures, and under what accounting, is unresolved, because the
  full text of the paper has not been read.

## Out of Scope

- The detailed structural design of the wing and the German certification arrangements behind it.
- The Vectoring Extremely Short Takeoff and Landing Control Tailless Operations Research programme
  of 2001 to 2003 in its own right, which is a distinct programme with distinct objectives and is
  treated here only where it bears on air data.
- The F/A-18 High Alpha Research Vehicle and the F-16 multi-axis thrust vectoring programme, both
  contemporaneous and both deserving separate treatment.
- Radar cross-section and low-observable design, which is the reason the tailless result matters
  and is not itself an X-31 subject.
- The design of the missiles the programme concluded were necessary.
- The organisational history of the International Test Organization beyond what bears on the
  flight-test method.

## Conclusion

**The X-31 was built to find out whether an aeroplane that can point its nose forty degrees further round than its opponent wins, and it found out that the answer depends on where the fight starts.**

The result is less satisfying than the reputation, and better. The programme produced four
exchange ratios against a conventional adversary and the aircraft lost two of them. It produced an overall
figure of 1.83, a loss-weighted average dominated by the two it lost, which sits three and a
half times below the average of the four.
**Between eighty-two and ninety-four percent of its simulated losses occurred in the conditions where post-stall manoeuvring did not help.**

It produced, in flight against front-line fighters, a clear advantage over the Navy types that would fight
it close and a clear disadvantage against the Air Force types that would not.

**An exchange ratio is not a property of an aeroplane. It is a property of an engagement**, and the
adversary has a say in which engagement occurs. The X-31 measured that with more care than anyone had
before, and the measurement is usually quoted as a single number by people who did not read the table it
came from.

**The programme also produced a result nobody was looking for that has outlasted the one it was built for.**
An aircraft with no vertical tail at all can be held at supersonic speed by vectoring, diverging at 290
milliseconds to double. Yaw control without a fin is now the central configuration problem of combat aircraft design and the X-31
answered it in 1994 as a side experiment made cheap by having already integrated vectoring into the control
laws.

**And it produced a lesson about instrumentation that cost an aeroplane.** A probe fitted to solve a real
problem at high angle of attack was not heated, its cockpit switch was not placarded, the hazard analysis
was not repeated, and the flight control system had no way to notice that both of its air data computers
were being fed the same wrong number. The information needed to catch it was displayed on the head-up
display, spoken aloud over the intercom, available on a standby instrument near the pilot's knee, and
computable in one line from the lift equation.
**None of those was a redundancy the design had asked for, and any one of them would have been enough.**
## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 71 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 71, 43 are established and 28 are bespoke.
Aircraft quantities are in customary units, with weights and thrusts in pounds, dynamic pressures in pounds per square foot, lengths in feet and speeds in knots or feet per second, every calibrated airspeed is read as the equivalent airspeed that gives the same dynamic pressure at sea-level density, and several letters are reused, so $n$ is a count of scored outcomes, a load factor and a thrust-lapse exponent, $\alpha$ is a significance level in the interval relations and the angle of attack elsewhere, $p$ and $r$ are a probability and a turn radius except in the velocity-vector roll relation, where they are body-axis roll and yaw rates, and $\rho_i$ is a campaign ratio rather than a density.

**Equation 1, Exchange Ratio.**
The exchange ratio is the number of adversary losses divided by the number of losses of the aircraft under test, a measure of effectiveness from the operations-research literature.
[measures of effectiveness for general-purpose forces][research_pugh_mayberry_1973]

$$
E = \frac{R}{B}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Arithmetic Mean of the Four Condition Ratios.**
The unweighted mean of the four published per-condition exchange ratios is 6.43, three and a half times the published overall figure.

$$
\bar{E} = \frac{0.36 + 8.5 + 16 + 0.86}{4} = 6.43
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Pooled Exchange Ratio as a Ratio of Sums.**
The pooled exchange ratio divides the total adversary losses by the total losses of the aircraft under test across all conditions.
[combining proportions across strata][research_hauck_anderson_1986]

$$
E_{\text{pool}} = \frac{\sum_i R_i}{\sum_i B_i}
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Pooled Ratio as a Loss-Weighted Mean.**
Substituting each condition's losses as its ratio times the test aircraft's losses shows the pooled ratio to be the mean of the condition ratios weighted by the denominator losses.
[combining proportions across strata][research_hauck_anderson_1986]

$$
E_{\text{pool}} = \frac{\sum_i E_i B_i}{\sum_i B_i}
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Pooled Ratio in Terms of Loss Shares.**
Writing the weights as each condition's share of the test aircraft's losses expresses the pooled ratio as a convex combination of the condition ratios.

$$
E_{\text{pool}} = \sum_i w_i E_i
\tag{5}
$$

*Equation 6, Bespoke Minimum Losing-Condition Share.*
The article bounds the share of losses in the losing conditions from below with a two-point mixture that places all winning weight on the smaller winning ratio and all losing weight on the smaller losing ratio.

$$
w_{\min} = \frac{E_{\text{win,min}} - E_{\text{pool}}}{E_{\text{win,min}} - E_{\text{lose,min}}} = \frac{8.5 - 1.83}{8.5 - 0.36} = 0.819
\tag{6}
$$

*Equation 7, Bespoke Maximum Losing-Condition Share.*
Pairing the two larger ratios in the same two-point construction gives the upper end of the bracket, 93.6 percent.

$$
w_{\max} = \frac{E_{\text{win,max}} - E_{\text{pool}}}{E_{\text{win,max}} - E_{\text{lose,max}}} = \frac{16 - 1.83}{16 - 0.86} = 0.936
\tag{7}
$$

*Equation 8, Bespoke Losing Share That Tips the Pooled Ratio to Parity.*
Solving the two-point mixture for a pooled ratio of exactly one gives a losing share of 92.14 percent, a threshold the article shows lies inside its bracket.

$$
w_{\text{tip}} = \frac{E_{\text{win,min}} - 1}{E_{\text{win,min}} - E_{\text{lose,min}}} = \frac{8.5 - 1}{8.5 - 0.36} = 0.9214
\tag{8}
$$

*Equation 9, Bespoke Two-Point Bracket on the Losing Share.*
The same two-point construction is stated in general form for application to the two further published comparisons.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
w_{\min} = \frac{E_{\text{win,min}} - E_{\text{pool}}}{E_{\text{win,min}} - E_{\text{lose,min}}} \qquad w_{\max} = \frac{E_{\text{win,max}} - E_{\text{pool}}}{E_{\text{win,max}} - E_{\text{lose,max}}}
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Exchange Ratio as Odds of a Bernoulli Outcome.**
If each scored outcome is a Bernoulli trial in which the adversary is lost with probability $p$, the exchange ratio is the odds $p/(1-p)$ and maps one to one onto that probability.
[Fleiss on statistical methods for rates and proportions][book_fleiss]
[Agresti on categorical data][book_agresti]

$$
E = \frac{p}{1 - p} \qquad \text{and} \qquad p = \frac{E}{1 + E}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Clopper-Pearson Lower Endpoint.**
The lower endpoint of the Clopper-Pearson interval is the probability at which the upper binomial tail from $k$ successes equals half the significance level.
[Clopper-Pearson interval][ref_clopper]

$$
\sum_{i=k}^{n} \binom{n}{i} p^{i} (1 - p)^{n - i} = \frac{\alpha}{2}
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Clopper-Pearson Upper Endpoint.**
The upper endpoint is the probability at which the lower binomial tail through $k$ successes equals half the significance level.
[Clopper-Pearson interval][ref_clopper]
[interval estimation for a binomial proportion][research_sandelius_1952]

$$
\sum_{i=0}^{k} \binom{n}{i} p^{i} (1 - p)^{n - i} = \frac{\alpha}{2}
\tag{12}
$$

*Equation 13, Bespoke Outcome Split Reconstructed From a Ratio.*
Because the counts are unpublished, the article reconstructs the adversary and test-aircraft losses from each published ratio and a stated number of scored outcomes that it sweeps.

$$
k = \operatorname{round}\left( \frac{n E}{1 + E} \right) \qquad \text{and} \qquad b = n - k
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Separation From Parity.**
A ratio is taken to separate from parity when its interval excludes one, which is the same as the interval on the probability excluding one half.

$$
\text{separates} \iff 1 \notin [E_{\text{lo}}, E_{\text{hi}}] \iff \tfrac{1}{2} \notin [p_{\text{lo}}, p_{\text{hi}}]
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Aspect Ratio From Span and Area.**
The aspect ratio implied by the published span and wing area is 2.509, against a published 2.51.

$$
A = \frac{b^{2}}{S} = \frac{23.83^{2}}{226.3} = 2.509
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Wing Loading at Normal Flying Weight.**
The normal flying weight divided by the wing area reproduces the published wing loading of 64.52 pounds per square foot.

$$
\frac{W}{S} = \frac{14{,}600}{226.3} = 64.52 \ \text{lb/ft}^{2}
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Lift Coefficient in Level Flight.**
In level flight the lift coefficient is the weight divided by dynamic pressure and wing area, with the dynamic pressure taken from calibrated airspeed at sea-level density.
[Etkin on the dynamics of flight][book_etkin]
[Nelson on flight stability][book_nelson]
[Cook on flight dynamics principles][book_cook]

$$
C_L = \frac{W}{q S} \qquad \text{with} \qquad q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_0 V_c^{2}
\tag{17}
$$

*Equation 18, Bespoke Lift-Curve Slope Inferred From a Pilot's Trim Point.*
The slope is inferred from a pilot's remark that twenty degrees corresponds to 135 to 140 knots, taking the midpoint of 137.5 knots, an assumed weight near 14,000 pounds and a lift line through the origin.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
C_{L\alpha} = 0.04833 \ \text{per degree} = 2.769 \ \text{per radian}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Helmbold Lift-Curve Slope.**
The Helmbold relation for a low-aspect-ratio unswept wing gives a lift-curve slope of 3.027 per radian at the published aspect ratio.

$$
C_{L\alpha} = \frac{\pi A}{1 + \sqrt{1 + (A/2)^{2}}} = \frac{\pi (2.51)}{1 + \sqrt{1 + 1.575}} = 3.027 \ \text{per radian}
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Swept-Wing Lift-Curve Slope at the Root Sweep.*
The handbook compressible form is evaluated at the root leading-edge sweep of 56.6 degrees, a single sweep the article takes for a cranked wing whose outboard panel is swept 45 degrees.
[stability and control handbook][ref_datcom]

$$
C_{L\alpha} = \frac{2 \pi A}{2 + \sqrt{\dfrac{A^{2} \beta^{2}}{\kappa^{2}} \left(1 + \dfrac{\tan^{2} \Lambda}{\beta^{2}}\right) + 4}} = 2.278 \ \text{per radian}
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Canard Contribution to the Lift-Curve Slope.**
A forward surface adds to the whole-aircraft slope in proportion to its area ratio and its own slope, scaled by an efficiency that accounts for upwash.

$$
\Delta C_{L\alpha} = \eta \, \frac{S_c}{S} \, C_{L\alpha,c}
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Yawing Moment From Thrust Vectoring.**
The yawing moment available from vectoring is the side component of thrust acting on the moment arm of the vanes.

$$
N_{\text{tv}} = T \sin \delta_j \, \ell_v
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Vectored Yawing Moment Coefficient.**
Dividing the vectored moment by dynamic pressure, wing area and span gives a coefficient that falls inversely with dynamic pressure.

$$
C_{n,\text{tv}} = \frac{T \sin \delta_j \, \ell_v}{q S b}
\tag{23}
$$

*Equation 24, Bespoke Upper Bound on the Vectoring Moment Arm.*
The article reads a departure as an asymmetry that exceeded the available authority, which turns the vectoring relation into an upper bound on the arm.
[asymmetry report][research_cobleigh_1994]

$$
\ell_v < \frac{C_{n0} \, q S b}{T \sin \delta_j}
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Dynamic Pressure at Mach 0.4 and 35,000 Feet.**
The dynamic pressure follows from the standard atmosphere pressure ratio and the quoted Mach number of the departure.

$$
q = \tfrac{\gamma}{2} \, p_0 \, \delta \, M^{2} = 0.7 \times 2{,}116.22 \times 0.2353 \times 0.4^{2} = 55.77 \ \text{psf}
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Arm Bound From the Departure.*
The bound of 36.2 feet uses the departure asymmetry of 0.125, a thrust of 16,000 pounds lapsed with the pressure ratio to the first power and a jet deflection of sixteen degrees, so the lapse exponent the article assumes governs it.

$$
\ell_v < \frac{0.125 \times 55.77 \times 226.3 \times 23.83}{3{,}765 \times \sin 16^{\circ}} = \frac{37{,}594}{1{,}037.8} = 36.2 \ \text{feet}
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Standard Troposphere Ratios.**
The 1976 standard troposphere gives the temperature ratio as linear in altitude, the pressure ratio as its 5.2559 power and the density ratio as their quotient.
[civil aviation atmosphere][ref_icao_atmosphere_1957]

$$
\theta = \frac{T}{T_0} = 1 - 6.87535 \times 10^{-6} \, h \qquad \delta = \frac{p}{p_0} = \theta^{5.2559} \qquad \sigma = \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \frac{\delta}{\theta}
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Speed of Sound From the Temperature Ratio.**
The speed of sound follows from the temperature alone and so from the sea-level value and the temperature ratio.

$$
a = \sqrt{\gamma R T} = \sqrt{\gamma R T_0 \theta}
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Thrust Lapse With Pressure Ratio.*
The article models thrust at fixed Mach number as the sea-level thrust times a power of the pressure ratio, taking an exponent near one and carrying it explicitly for sensitivity.
[Bronz et al. 2017][research_bronz_garciademarina_2017]
[identified engine performance models][research_andrianantara_ghazi_2021]

$$
T(h) = T_{\text{SL}} \, \delta(h)^{n}
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Moment Arm Needed to Hold an Asymmetry.**
Solving the vectoring relation at equality gives the moment arm needed to balance a given asymmetric yawing moment coefficient.

$$
\ell_{\text{req}} = \frac{C_{n0} \, q S b}{T \sin \delta_j}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Needed Arms at Two Flight Conditions.*
Two table entries are worked with the steady asymmetry bound of 0.080 and thrusts lapsed under the assumed pressure-ratio model.

$$
\ell_{\text{req}}^{20{,}000,\,150} = \frac{0.080 \times 76.2 \times 226.3 \times 23.83}{7{,}353 \times \sin 16^{\circ}} = \frac{32{,}874}{2{,}026.8} = 16.2 \ \text{ft} \qquad \ell_{\text{req}}^{30{,}000,\,250} = \frac{0.080 \times 211.6 \times 226.3 \times 23.83}{4{,}751 \times \sin 16^{\circ}} = \frac{91{,}288}{1{,}309.6} = 69.7 \ \text{ft}
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Dynamic Pressure Above Which No Arm Suffices.*
Setting the needed arm equal to the fuselage length, a geometric ceiling the article imposes, gives the dynamic pressure and calibrated airspeed above which vectoring cannot hold the asymmetry.

$$
q_{L} = \frac{L \, T \sin \delta_j}{C_{n0} \, S b} \qquad V_{c,L} = \sqrt{\frac{2 q_{L}}{\rho_0}}
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Ceiling Speed at 20,000 Feet Against the Departure Asymmetry.*
At twenty thousand feet with the lapsed thrust and the departure asymmetry of 0.125, the ceiling falls at 190 knots.

$$
q_{L} = \frac{40.67 \times 7{,}353 \times \sin 16^{\circ}}{0.125 \times 226.3 \times 23.83} = \frac{82{,}428}{674.09} = 122.3 \ \text{psf} \qquad V_{c,L} = 320.8 \ \text{ft/s} = 190.0 \ \text{knots}
\tag{33}
$$

**Equation 34, Equivalent Airspeed of the Departure.**
The dynamic pressure of the departure condition corresponds at sea-level density to an equivalent airspeed of 128.3 knots.

$$
V_e = \sqrt{\frac{2 q}{\rho_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 55.77}{0.0023769}} = 216.6 \ \text{ft/s} = 128.3 \ \text{knots}
\tag{34}
$$

**Equation 35, Measured Swing in Asymmetric Yawing Moment.**
The asymmetry report records a swing from 0.077 in one direction to 0.088 in the other, a change of 0.165 within three degrees of angle of attack.
[asymmetry report][research_cobleigh_1994]

$$
\Delta C_n = 0.165 \ \text{across three degrees of angle of attack}
\tag{35}
$$

**Equation 36, Asymmetric Yawing Moment From Its Coefficient.**
The dimensional yawing moment is the coefficient times dynamic pressure, wing area and span.

$$
N_{0} = C_{n0} \, q S b
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Altitude Ratio of Vectored Authority.*
At constant calibrated airspeed the unknown arm cancels and the vectored authority scales with thrust, which the article approximates by the ratio of pressure ratios under its lapse model.

$$
\frac{C_{n,\text{tv}}(h_2)}{C_{n,\text{tv}}(h_1)} = \frac{T(h_2)}{T(h_1)} \approx \frac{\delta(h_2)}{\delta(h_1)}
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Radius of a Level Turn.**
The radius of a level turn is the speed squared divided by gravity times the square root of load factor squared less one.

$$
r = \frac{V^{2}}{g \sqrt{n^{2} - 1}}
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Available Load Factor.**
The load factor is the lift the wing can produce divided by the weight.

$$
n = \frac{q S C_L}{W}
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Slowest Level-Flight Speed at a Given Lift Coefficient.**
Setting the load factor to one gives the slowest equivalent airspeed at which the aircraft can hold a given lift coefficient in level flight.

$$
V_{\text{level}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 W}{\rho_0 S C_L}}
\tag{40}
$$

*Equation 41, Bespoke Level-Flight Speed at Seventy Degrees.*
The level-flight speed of 138 knots rests on a lift coefficient of 1.00 at seventy degrees of angle of attack, an estimate the article makes rather than a measurement.

$$
V_{\text{level}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 14{,}600}{0.0023769 \times 226.3 \times 1.00}} = 233.0 \ \text{ft/s} = 138.0 \ \text{knots}
\tag{41}
$$

*Equation 42, Bespoke Aim Angle Bought by Post-Stall Flight.*
The article measures the capability as the difference between the seventy-degree post-stall limit and a conventional limit it takes as thirty degrees.

$$
\Delta \psi_{\text{aim}} = \alpha_{\max} - \alpha_{\text{conv}} = 70 - 30 = 40 \ \text{degrees}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Time to Turn Through an Angle.**
The time to turn the velocity vector through an angle is that angle divided by the level-turn rate, which follows from speed and load factor.

$$
t = \frac{\Delta \psi}{\omega} \qquad \text{with} \qquad \omega = \frac{g \sqrt{n^{2} - 1}}{V}
\tag{43}
$$

**Equation 44, Corner Speed.**
The corner speed is the speed at which the lift limit meets the structural load factor limit.
[corner speed][ref_corner_speed]
[Anderson on aircraft performance and design][book_anderson_perf]
[Raymer on conceptual design][book_raymer]

$$
V^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 n_{\max} W}{\rho_0 S C_{L\max}}}
\tag{44}
$$

**Equation 45, Specific Energy.**
Specific energy, or energy height, is altitude plus the kinetic energy per unit weight.

$$
E_s = h + \frac{V^{2}}{2 g}
\tag{45}
$$

*Equation 46, Bespoke True Airspeeds at Corner Speed and Post-Stall Exit.*
The true airspeeds at twenty thousand feet are found from equivalent airspeeds whose corner value rests on the lift coefficient of 1.4498 taken from the inferred lift curve.

$$
V = \frac{V_e}{\sqrt{\sigma}} \qquad V^{*} = \frac{580.5}{\sqrt{0.5328}} = 795.3 \ \text{ft/s} = 471.2 \ \text{knots} \qquad V_1 = \frac{202.5}{\sqrt{0.5328}} = 277.5 \ \text{ft/s} = 164.4 \ \text{knots}
\tag{46}
$$

*Equation 47, Bespoke Energy Lost Falling From Corner Speed.*
The specific energy given up between the inferred corner speed and an exit at 120 knots is about 8,630 feet.

$$
\Delta E_s = \frac{V^{*2} - V_1^{2}}{2 g} = \frac{795.3^{2} - 277.5^{2}}{2 \times 32.174} = \frac{555{,}496}{64.348} = 8{,}630 \ \text{feet}
\tag{47}
$$

**Equation 48, Specific Excess Power With a Parabolic Polar.**
Specific excess power is speed times the excess of thrust over drag divided by weight, with drag from a parabolic polar.
[energy-manoeuvrability comparison][research_johnson_1972]

$$
P_s = \frac{V (T - D)}{W} \qquad \text{with} \qquad D = q S \left( C_{D0} + \frac{C_L^{2}}{\pi A e} \right)
\tag{48}
$$

*Equation 49, Bespoke Specific Excess Power at the Slow End.*
The slow-end figure of 68.6 feet per second uses a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.022 and an efficiency factor of 0.70, both values the article assumes, with lapsed thrust.

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_0 \sigma V_1^{2} = 48.75 \ \text{psf} \qquad C_L = \frac{14{,}600}{48.75 \times 226.3} = 1.323 \qquad P_s = \frac{277.5 \, (7{,}353 - 3{,}743)}{14{,}600} = 68.6 \ \text{ft/s}
\tag{49}
$$

*Equation 50, Bespoke Specific Excess Power at the Fast End.*
The fast-end figure of 268.7 feet per second uses the same assumed drag polar and lapsed thrust.

$$
q = 400.5 \ \text{psf} \qquad C_L = \frac{14{,}600}{400.5 \times 226.3} = 0.161 \qquad P_s = \frac{795.3 \, (7{,}353 - 2{,}420)}{14{,}600} = 268.7 \ \text{ft/s}
\tag{50}
$$

*Equation 51, Bespoke Integrated Energy Recovery Time.*
Integrating the reciprocal of specific excess power over speed on the assumed polar gives 46.0 seconds, against 125.8 seconds from a single-point estimate at the slow end.

$$
t = \int_{V_1}^{V^{*}} \frac{V \, dV}{g \, P_s(V)} = 46.0 \ \text{s} \qquad \text{against} \qquad \frac{\Delta E_s}{P_s(V_1)} = \frac{8{,}632.7}{68.60} = 125.8 \ \text{s}
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Roll Rate About the Velocity Vector.**
A roll about the velocity vector combines body-axis roll and yaw rates weighted by the cosine and sine of the angle of attack.
[review of high angle of attack control system performance][research_huberpeter_seamountpatricia_1994]

$$
p_w = p \cos \alpha + r \sin \alpha
\tag{52}
$$

**Equation 53, Roll and Yaw Weights at Seventy Degrees.**
At seventy degrees the cosine and sine weights are 0.3420 and 0.9397, so a velocity-vector roll is mostly yaw rate.

$$
\cos 70^{\circ} = 0.3420 \qquad \sin 70^{\circ} = 0.9397
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Amplitude at Which an Actuator Rate Limit Binds.**
A sinusoidal command of amplitude $A$ at frequency $\omega$ demands a peak rate of $A\omega$, so the rate limit binds above the amplitude equal to the maximum rate over the frequency.

$$
A_{\text{bind}} = \frac{\dot{\delta}_{\max}}{\omega}
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Eigenvalue From a Time to Double.**
A divergent mode growing as $e^{\lambda t}$ has an eigenvalue equal to the natural logarithm of two over the time to double, here 2.39 per second from the published 290 milliseconds.
[statically unstable configurations under displacement and rate saturation][research_hanson_stengel_1981]

$$
\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_2} = \frac{0.6931}{0.290} = 2.3902 \ \text{per second}
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Yaw Divergence Eigenvalue and Directional Stiffness.**
For a yaw-only divergence the square of the eigenvalue is minus the directional stiffness moment divided by the yaw inertia.
[flight measurement of lateral and directional stability][research_cranehl_reederjp_1945]

$$
\lambda^{2} = -\frac{q S b \, C_{n\beta}}{I_z}
\tag{56}
$$

**Equation 57, True Airspeed, Equivalent Airspeed and Dynamic Pressure.**
True airspeed is Mach number times the speed of sound, equivalent airspeed scales it by the square root of the density ratio, and both routes give the same dynamic pressure.
[Altman 1952][research_altman_1952]

$$
V_{\text{true}} = M a \qquad V_{\text{eq}} = V_{\text{true}} \sqrt{\sigma} \qquad q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_0 \sigma V_{\text{true}}^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_0 V_{\text{eq}}^{2}
\tag{57}
$$

**Equation 58, Directional Stiffness per Unit Yaw Inertia.**
The published doubling time fixes the ratio of directional stiffness to yaw inertia, here evaluated at thirty thousand feet, without fixing either factor.

$$
-\frac{C_{n\beta}}{I_z} = 1.6724 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{per slug foot squared per radian}
\tag{58}
$$

**Equation 59, Delay Bound for a First-Order Unstable Plant.**
A first-order unstable plant with a pure delay cannot be stabilised by proportional feedback once the delay approaches the reciprocal of the unstable pole.

$$
\tau_{\max} \approx \frac{1}{\lambda}
\tag{59}
$$

**Equation 60, Impact Pressure of a Pitot-Static Probe.**
The impact pressure is total minus static pressure, which for subsonic flow follows from the isentropic relation in Mach number.

$$
q_c = p_t - p_s = p_0 \left[ \left( 1 + \tfrac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}} - 1 \right]
\tag{60}
$$

*Equation 61, Bespoke Loop Gain Error From an Airspeed Error.*
The article models the gain schedule as reducing gain with indicated dynamic pressure while surface effectiveness follows true dynamic pressure, so the loop gain is multiplied by the square of the airspeed ratio.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
\frac{K_{\text{actual}}}{K_{\text{design}}} = \frac{q_{\text{true}}}{q_{\text{indicated}}} = \left( \frac{V_{\text{true}}}{V_{\text{indicated}}} \right)^{2}
\tag{61}
$$

**Equation 62, Gain Ratio in Decibels.**
A gain ratio is expressed in decibels as twenty times its common logarithm.

$$
\text{dB} = 20 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{actual}}}{K_{\text{design}}} \right)
\tag{62}
$$

*Equation 63, Bespoke Angle of Attack Implied by Airspeed in Level Flight.*
The angle of attack implied by an indicated airspeed at one g uses the lift-curve slope inferred from the pilot's trim point with a lift line through the origin.

$$
\alpha = \frac{W}{q S C_{L\alpha}}
\tag{63}
$$

*Equation 64, Bespoke Disagreement Between Vane and Airspeed.*
The disagreements of 11.2 and 6.9 degrees compare the twenty degrees read on the vane with the angles implied at 207 and 170 knots by the inferred lift curve.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
\Delta \alpha_{207} = 20.00 - 8.82 = 11.2 \ \text{degrees} \qquad \Delta \alpha_{170} = 20.00 - 13.08 = 6.9 \ \text{degrees}
\tag{64}
$$

*Equation 65, Bespoke Display Error Against a Six-Decibel Margin.*
The display error is measured against 137.5 knots, the midpoint of the pilot's stated range of 135 to 140 knots, and compared in dynamic pressure with a conventional six-decibel margin.

$$
\frac{207}{137.5} = 1.505 \qquad \left( \frac{207}{137.5} \right)^{2} = 2.266 \qquad 10^{6/20} = 1.995
\tag{65}
$$

**Equation 66, Flight Rate and Flights per Flying Day.**
The flight rate is the number of flights over the elapsed time, and flights per flying day divides the same count by the number of distinct flying days.

$$
\dot{N} = \frac{N}{\Delta t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{N}{D} = \text{flights per flying day}
\tag{66}
$$

**Equation 67, Scored Fractions of Sorties and Engagements.**
The published counts give 92.0 percent of tactical sorties scored and 79.9 percent of engagements scored.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
\frac{80}{87} = 92.0 \ \text{percent of sorties scored} \qquad \frac{325}{407} = 79.9 \ \text{percent of engagements scored}
\tag{67}
$$

**Equation 68, Engagements per Scored Sortie.**
The published counts give about five engagements and four scored engagements per scored sortie.
[available in full][ref_joyce_pdf]

$$
\frac{407}{80} = 5.09 \ \text{engagements per scored sortie} \qquad \frac{325}{80} = 4.06 \ \text{scored engagements per scored sortie}
\tag{68}
$$

*Equation 69, Bespoke Campaign Repeatability Ratio.*
The article measures the repeatability of the two simulation campaigns by the ratio of their exchange ratios condition by condition.

$$
\rho_i = \frac{E_i^{\text{I}}}{E_i^{\text{II}}}
\tag{69}
$$

*Equation 70, Bespoke Repeatability Ratios and Ratio of Campaign Means.*
Evaluating the repeatability ratios and the ratio of the unweighted campaign means shows closer agreement in aggregate than in any single condition.

$$
1 - \frac{22}{23} = 0.043 \qquad \frac{20}{6.67} = 2.999 \qquad \frac{2.8}{1.5} = 1.867 \qquad \frac{\bar{E}^{\text{I}}}{\bar{E}^{\text{II}}} = \frac{(1.2 + 22 + 20 + 1.5)/4}{(0.47 + 23 + 6.67 + 2.8)/4} = \frac{11.175}{8.235} = 1.357
\tag{70}
$$

*Equation 71, Bespoke Condition for Pooling to Reverse a Conclusion.*
The article states the reversal condition as an unweighted mean of condition ratios above parity together with a loss-weighted pooled ratio below it.

$$
\frac{1}{N} \sum_i E_i > 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_i w_i E_i < 1
\tag{71}
$$

### Notation

- $E$, the exchange ratio, with $E_i$ the ratio in condition $i$ and $E_{\text{pool}}$ the pooled ratio
- $w_i$, the share of the test aircraft's losses in condition $i$
- $k$, the number of adversary losses in $n$ scored outcomes
- $A$, the wing aspect ratio, except in the actuator relation, where it is a command amplitude
- $S$, the wing reference area, with $S_c$ the canard area
- $b$, the wing span, except in the reconstructed split, where it is the number of test aircraft losses
- $W$, the weight
- $C_L$, the lift coefficient
- $C_{L\alpha}$, the lift-curve slope
- $q$, the dynamic pressure
- $\rho_0$, the sea-level air density
- $\delta_j$, the jet deflection angle
- $\ell_v$, the moment arm of the thrust-vectoring vanes
- $C_{n0}$, the asymmetric yawing moment coefficient
- $\theta$, the temperature ratio of the standard atmosphere
- $\delta$, the pressure ratio of the standard atmosphere
- $\sigma$, the density ratio of the standard atmosphere
- $V^{*}$, the corner speed
- $E_s$, the specific energy
- $P_s$, the specific excess power
- $C_{D0}$, the zero-lift drag coefficient
- $\lambda$, the eigenvalue of a divergent mode
- $C_{n\beta}$, the directional stability derivative
- $I_z$, the moment of inertia in yaw
- $q_c$, the impact pressure
- $K_{\text{actual}}$, the loop gain in flight, with $K_{\text{design}}$ the gain the schedule intends
